accuracy.evidence: Definitions follow the Met Office and WMO usage: weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place and time; climate is the long-term average, computed as a 30-year climate normal (WMO-No. 1203; current period 1991 to 2020). London monthly rainfall bars are the Heathrow 1991 to 2020 normals rounded (55, 41, 42, 44, 49, 45, 45, 50, 49, 69, 59, 55 mm); Singapore (Changi) and Cairo bars are rounded normals, Cairo near zero from May to September. The July and January series are labelled in the adult text as made-up years close to London's real averages (July mean high about 23 °C, January about 8 °C). The January arithmetic was recomputed: mean 7.16 °C, and 6.81 °C after day 15 becomes −4 °C; the 30-July mean is 22.3 °C.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented confusions (Met Office and NASA Climate Kids teaching notes; Shepardson et al. 2009 on students' conceptions of weather and climate): treating weather and climate as the same (challenge 'same', m8, sorter), one cold or snowy day disproving a climate (challenge 'one', p3, step 3 prediction), one hot spell proving change (step 2 prediction, m3), climate as a week or a season (challenge 'short', m1), mixing up long-pattern and short-term statements (challenge 'swap', m2, p1) and using a climate graph as a forecast (step 5, challenge 'tool', p5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagwxclim is about the time scale that separates weather from climate: face-down day cards revealing a week of changing April weather, a 30-year July high chart whose running average line barely moves past a red 26 °C heatwave bar, a draggable January day whose effect on the monthly average is shown live, three real rainfall climate graphs to label, and a forecast-versus-climate-record decision board. flagwxtype names weather types, flagcloud and flagwind explain single weather processes; none averages records over years. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children discover the idea before the text names it: the week shows three kinds of sky and 8 to 15 °C; adding years one block at a time shows the average settling near 22 °C while the heatwave bar stands out; dragging day 15 from 7 °C to −4 °C moves the January line only from 7.2 to 6.8 °C; the graphs show each place's usual rain; and wrong board choices explain why a forecast or a climate record is needed.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'it stays the same all week' (the cards change daily), 'the climate is hotter now' after one heatwave July (the average stays near 22 °C), 'it falls a lot, close to −4 °C' for one freezing day (it falls by about 0.35 °C), and 'Yes, it rained, so it is wet' for Cairo (its graph shows almost no rain).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions; each wrong option carries one of five distinct messages that name the slip: one day taken as climate, weather and climate treated as the same, a week mistaken for the climate time span, short-term and usual-pattern wording swapped, and a climate graph used as a forecast. Answer order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and everyday words (look out of the window, the usual weather of a place) and give one idea each; the adult text names the KS1 and KS2 geography wording, NGSS 3-ESS2-1 and 3-ESS2-2 and the key vocabulary. Canvas labels are a few words. The lab uses the young layout with 56 px buttons. validate_lessons readability passes.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph adds something new: weather now, how fast it changes, climate from 30 years, three real climates, one odd day, forecast versus climate. Items mix identifying weather statements (p1, m2), the 30-year span (p2, m1), single events (p3, m3, m8), day-to-day change in numbers (p4, m4, m7), choosing a forecast (p5, m6) and reading a climate (m5, m9).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and 360 px Android dark screenshots of every step at the start and after Show me. The 7 day cards fit at 360 px with readable day names and temperatures; the July chart has its own 16 to 28 °C scale so the heatwave bar stands out and the average chip sits above the bars; the January drag dot is enlarged on phones with a 44 px hit radius; the three graphs keep their names and tags readable; used tags turn light grey with dark ink in both themes.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: Open the next day; Add 5 more years; Colder by 2 °C and Warmer by 2 °C; one button per graph and label pair; Weather forecast and Climate record. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with the day's weather, the running July average, the new January average, why a label does or does not fit, and the answer to each question. walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
